own_scenes.desc: En agosto de 1966 la violencia dejó de ser un hecho aislado para convertirse en clima. El 1 de agosto Charles Whitman, estudiante de veinticinco años, mató a dieciséis personas desde la torre de la Universidad de Texas: Time lo presentó como un nuevo enemigo interior, el psicótico «chico americano». El 5 de agosto una turba blanca de 5.000 personas recibió a pedradas a Martin Luther King en Marquette Park (Chicago), donde días después hizo un mitin el Partido Nazi americano; hubo disturbios raciales en ciudad tras ciudad. En Reino Unido, el juicio de los asesinos de los páramos (Brady y Hindley, mayo) y el asesinato de tres policías en Braybrook Street (12 de agosto), muy lejos del Swinging London, horrorizaron al país.

refs.q: A blistering hostility was in the air during August 1966.
refs.para: A blistering hostility was in the air during August 1966. There was a sense of matters coming to a head, as the pressure rose with the heat and violence became not a random event, but a climate. There were many words expended on causes and reasons, but the purple and black heart of that turbulent season was definitively evoked not by a literary insider or a New Journalist, but by the taboo-busting novelist John Rechy.

refs.q: This was a new stain upon America.
refs.para: This was a new stain upon America. Charles Whitman presented himself as an unprecedented kind of enemy within – all the more disturbing because he was so apparently ‘a real all-American boy’. Previously unrecognised and still ill-defined, the psychotic was added to the cluster of enemies and subversives that appeared to be threatening the country’s way of life: war protestors, assertive Black Power ideologues, homosexuals.
